\chapter{Profesor --- and the Article Spanish Leaves Out}
\label{ch:profesor}
\hlchaptermodality{51}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what someone does for a living with ser and no article.}

I can say what someone does for a living with ser and no article.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[profesor]{profesor}

\label{lesson:ES-C09-profesor}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}I am.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Soy}.) You learned \emph{ser} three chapters ago as the verb for saying \textbf{what someone is}.

And then you had nothing to put after it. Today you do.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{profesor}} — a teacher
\end{quote}

Latin \textbf{profitērī} meant to \emph{declare something publicly}. A \emph{profesor} is someone who has declared what they know — which is also why in English you \textbf{profess} a faith, and why the work you declare yourself trained in is a \textbf{profession}.

\begin{quote}
\emph{profesor} $\leftarrow$ \emph{profitērī} $\to$ \textbf{professor}, \textbf{profess}, \textbf{profession}
\end{quote}

Say it: \emph{profesor}. And for a woman, \emph{profesora}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the missing \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{}}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{After \emph{ser}, a job takes no \emph{un} or \emph{una}.}
\end{quote}

You learned \emph{un} and \emph{una} early, and you have been right to use them. Here is the one place Spanish leaves them out.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\emph{Soy profesor.} & I am \textbf{a} teacher. \\
\emph{Es profesora.} & She is \textbf{a} teacher. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English needs the \emph{a}. Spanish does not — because it is not counting one teacher, it is naming what kind of person you are.

\emph{Soy un profesor} is not wrong so much as \textbf{different}: it makes the teacher into one item out of several, the way English does with \emph{I'm a teacher, not the teacher}. Say the bare one and you will sound like everyone else.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Soy profesor}
  \item \emph{Trabajo} — and now say what you are
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What word does English need here that Spanish leaves out? (\emph{\textbf{a}}.)

Now say what you are, out loud, even if it is not \emph{profesor} yet.
\end{tcolorbox}
